'''Stephan W. Koch''' (23 May 1953 in [[Frankfurt am Main]] – 12 September 2022 in [[Fronhausen]]<ref>{{cite web|title=Wir trauern um Stephan W. Koch|periodical=|publisher=Fachbereich Physik der [[Universität Marburg]]|url=https://www.uni-marburg.de/de/fb13/aktuelles/nachrichten/2022/nachruf|format=|access-date=5 October 2022|last=|date=4 October 2022|language=|pages=|quote=}}</ref><ref>Ada Bäumner, Rolf Binder, Sangam Chatterjee, Weng Chow, Harald Giessen, Jörg Hader, Hartmut Haug, Martin Hofmann, Frank Jahnke, Mackillo Kira, Andreas Knorr, Martin Koch, Markus Lindberg, Torsten Meier, Jerome V. Moloney, Hans Christian Schneider, Angela Thränhardt, Peter Thomas, Tineke Warncke: ''Nachruf auf Stephan W. Koch.'' In: [[Physik Journal]] 21 (2022), Nr. 11, S. 47.</ref><ref>Menschen, Verstorbene. In: [[Physik Journal]] 21 (2022), Nr. 11, S. 45.</ref>) was a German theoretical physicist. He was a professor at the [[University of Marburg]] and works on [[condensed matter theory|condensed-matter theory]], [[many-body]] effects, and [[laser]] theory. He is best known for his seminal contributions to the optical and electronic properties of [[semiconductors]], semiconductor [[quantum optics]], and semiconductor [[laser]] designs. Major portion of his research work has focused on the [[quantum physics]] and application potential of [[semiconductor]] [[nanostructures]]. Besides gaining fundamental insights to the many-body quantum theory, his work has provided new possibilities to develop, e.g., laser technology, based on accurate [[computer simulations]]. His objective has been to self-consistently include all relevant many-body effects in order to eliminate [[Phenomenology (particle physics)|phenomenological]] approximations that compromise predictability of effects and quantum-device designs.

==Biography==
Stephan W. Koch studied physics at the [[Goethe University Frankfurt|University of Frankfurt]],<ref name="IEEE Xplore 2021">{{cite web |title=Stephan W. Koch | website=IEEE Xplore | date=30 November 2021 | url=https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/author/37274646200 | access-date=16 December 2021}}</ref> obtained his doctorate 1979 about the theory of [[electron]]–[[electron hole|hole]] droplet [[nucleation]] in strongly excited [[semiconductors]]<ref name="SWKdiss">Koch, S. W. (1979). ''Zur Theorie der Elektron-Loch-Tropfennukleation in stark angeregten Halbleitern'' (PhD). Johann Wolfgang Goethe-Universität Frankfurt am Main (Germany).</ref> under the supervision of Hartmut Haug.<ref name="www.internal-interfaces.de – SFB1083">{{cite web | title=CV – Stephan Koch – www.internal-interfaces.de | website=www.internal-interfaces.de – SFB1083 | url=https://www.internal-interfaces.de/cv-stephan-koch/ | access-date=16 December 2021}}</ref> During 1981–83, he was a postdoctoral fellow and visiting scientist at the [[IBM Research]], [[San Jose, California|San Jose]]/California and received [[habilitation]] in 1983 about the dynamics of equilibrium and non-equilibrium first-order [[phase transitions]],<ref name="SWKhabil">Koch, S. W. (1983). ''Zur Dynamik von Gleichgewichts- und Nichtgleichgewichtsphasenübergängen erster Ordnung'' (Habilitation Thesis). Johann Wolfgang Goethe-Universität Frankfurt am Main (Germany).</ref> from the Department of Theoretical Physics of the University of Frankfurt. He continued his active research both in Germany and US with the help of scholarships from the F. Thyssen Foundation and of the Heisenberg Program of the [[Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft]]. In 1986, he became professor at the Physics Department and [[University of Arizona College of Optical Sciences|Optical Sciences Center]] of the [[University of Arizona]] in [[Tucson]], [[Arizona|AZ]], and in 1989, he accepted a chair there. In 1993, he accepted a chair of theoretical physics at the [[University of Marburg]], where he has worked ever since.<ref name="Philipps-Universität Marburg 2010">{{cite web | title=Lebenslauf – AG Theoretische Halbleiterphysik – Sekretariat: R. Schmid | website=Philipps-Universität Marburg | date=18 February 2010 | url=https://www.uni-marburg.de/fb13/forschungsgruppen/theoretische-halbleiterphysik/mitglieder/koch/lebenslauf | language=de | access-date=16 December 2021}}</ref> Stephan W. Koch has very close ties with the research efforts at the [[University of Arizona College of Optical Sciences|Optical Sciences Center]], University of Arizona, where he has been an [[adjunct professor]] and an active collaborator since 1994.<ref name="Philipps-Universität Marburg 2010" />

==Main research topics==

Stephan W. Koch has worked on multiple topics in the general field of semiconductor optics. Before the year 1988, the state-of-the-art description of semiconductor optics and lasers was mainly based on simplified [[Rate equation|rate-equation]] approaches which cannot describe the nonequilibrium quantum kinetics of Coulomb-coupled electrons and holes (electronic vacancies in [[valence band]]). To go beyond this approach, he was one of the key players to develop the [[semiconductor Bloch equations]] (abbreviated as SBEs).<ref name="Lindberg Koch pp. 3342–3350">{{cite journal | last1=Lindberg | first1=M. | last2=Koch | first2=S. W. | title=Effective Bloch equations for semiconductors | journal=Physical Review B | publisher=American Physical Society (APS) | volume=38 | issue=5 | date=15 August 1988 | issn=0163-1829 | doi=10.1103/physrevb.38.3342 | pages=3342–3350| pmid=9946675 | bibcode=1988PhRvB..38.3342L }}</ref>
<ref name="Haug Koch 2009 p. ">{{cite book | last1=Haug | first1=Hartmut | last2=Koch | first2=Stephan W | title=Quantum Theory of the Optical and Electronic Properties of Semiconductors | publisher=WORLD SCIENTIFIC | year=2009 | isbn=978-981-283-883-4 | doi=10.1142/7184 | page=}}</ref>
Ever since this breakthrough, the SBEs have been expanded to systematically include new many-body effects such as excitation-induced dephasing,<ref name="Kira Koch 2009 p. ">{{cite book | last1=Kira | first1=Mackillo | last2=Koch | first2=Stephan W. | title=Semiconductor Quantum Optics | publisher=Cambridge University Press | publication-place=Cambridge | year=2009 | isbn=978-1-139-01692-6 | doi=10.1017/cbo9781139016926 | page=}}</ref>
<ref name="Wang Ferrio Steel Hu pp. 1261–1264">{{cite journal | last1=Wang | first1=Hailin | last2=Ferrio | first2=Kyle | last3=Steel | first3=Duncan G. | last4=Hu | first4=Y. Z. | last5=Binder | first5=R. | last6=Koch | first6=S. W. | title=Transient nonlinear optical response from excitation induced dephasing in GaAs | journal=Physical Review Letters | publisher=American Physical Society (APS) | volume=71 | issue=8 | date=23 August 1993 | issn=0031-9007 | doi=10.1103/physrevlett.71.1261 | pages=1261–1264| pmid=10055491 | bibcode=1993PhRvL..71.1261W }}</ref>
[[Markov process|non-Markovian]] effects, and semiconductor excitations with [[Terahertz radiation|terahertz]] (abbreviated as THz)
fields.<ref name="Koch Kira Khitrova Gibbs 2006 pp. 523–531">{{cite journal | last1=Koch | first1=S. W. | last2=Kira | first2=M. | last3=Khitrova | first3=G. | last4=Gibbs | first4=H. M. | title=Semiconductor excitons in new light | journal=Nature Materials | publisher=Springer Science and Business Media LLC | volume=5 | issue=7 | year=2006 | issn=1476-1122 | doi=10.1038/nmat1658 | pages=523–531| pmid=16819475 | bibcode=2006NatMa...5..523K | s2cid=6313330 }}</ref>
The SBEs research is still very active, and the SBEs are the most sophisticated and successful approach to describe optical properties of semiconductors originating
from the classical light–matter interaction.

During the late 1980s, [[Quantum dot|quantum-dot]] systems started to catch a significant research attention worldwide due to their intriguing [[Potential well|quantum-confinement]] properties. He and his coworkers demonstrated<ref name="Hu Lindberg Koch pp. 1713–1723">{{cite journal | last1=Hu | first1=Y. Z. | last2=Lindberg | first2=M. | last3=Koch | first3=S. W. | title=Theory of optically excited intrinsic semiconductor quantum dots | journal=Physical Review B | publisher=American Physical Society (APS) | volume=42 | issue=3 | date=15 July 1990 | issn=0163-1829 | doi=10.1103/physrevb.42.1713 | pages=1713–1723| pmid=9995602 | bibcode=1990PhRvB..42.1713H }}</ref>
the configuration-interaction approach and its application to the optical properties of strongly quantum-confined semiconductors. This approach is actively used in order to explain the quantum-optical properties of quantum-dot systems.

Several of his ongoing projects focus on problems arising in the area of modern semiconductor [[quantum optics]], [[Optical microcavity|microcavities]], and [[semiconductor laser theory|laser theory]].<ref name="Khitrova Gibbs Kira Koch 2006 pp. 81–90">{{cite journal | last1=Khitrova | first1=G. | last2=Gibbs | first2=H. M. | last3=Kira | first3=M. | last4=Koch | first4=S. W. | last5=Scherer | first5=A. | title=Vacuum Rabi splitting in semiconductors | journal=Nature Physics | publisher=Springer Science and Business Media LLC | volume=2 | issue=2 | year=2006 | issn=1745-2473 | doi=10.1038/nphys227 | pages=81–90| bibcode=2006NatPh...2...81K | s2cid=120835659 }}</ref>
In this field, Stephan W. Koch and his coworkers have concentrated on explaining how the quantum features of light can be described in connection with semiconductors. The novelty and difficulty of this research stems from determining and controlling many-body and quantum-optical features simultaneously. The first step toward this direction emerged in the form of the [[semiconductor luminescence equations]]<ref name="Kira Jahnke Koch Berger pp. 5170–5173">{{cite journal | last1=Kira | first1=M. | last2=Jahnke | first2=F. | last3=Koch | first3=S. W. | last4=Berger | first4=J. D. | last5=Wick | first5=D. V. | last6=Nelson | first6=T. R. | last7=Khitrova | first7=G. | last8=Gibbs | first8=H. M. | title=Quantum Theory of Nonlinear Semiconductor Microcavity Luminescence Explaining "Boser" Experiments | journal=Physical Review Letters | publisher=American Physical Society (APS) | volume=79 | issue=25 | date=22 December 1997 | issn=0031-9007 | doi=10.1103/physrevlett.79.5170 | pages=5170–5173| bibcode=1997PhRvL..79.5170K }}</ref>
(abbreviated as SLEs); the SLEs describe the quantum physics where quantum fluctuations of light initiate [[Coherence (physics)|incoherent]] light emission from [[Spontaneous emission|spontaneous]] recombination of [[Coulomb]]-coupled electron–hole pairs. The SLEs not only set the standard in describing quantum-light emission in semiconductors but they are also ideally suited for modeling quantum-light sources and filters based on
semiconductor technology. The extensions of SLEs include [[resonance fluorescence]] and higher-order photon-correlation effects and are the basis to expand the [[quantum-optical spectroscopy]].

He and his coworkers are working on a systematic theory to describe excitation of solids with THz fields. Typical laser excitations are resonant with band-to-band transitions, not the energy difference of several relevant many-body states that actually match the THz-photon energy. Therefore, THz spectroscopy offers a new way to view many-body systems, e.g.,  by detecting particular many-body states<ref name="Kira Hoyer Stroucken Koch p. ">{{cite journal | last1=Kira | first1=M. | last2=Hoyer | first2=W. | last3=Stroucken | first3=T. | last4=Koch | first4=S. W. | title=Exciton Formation in Semiconductors and the Influence of a Photonic Environment | journal=Physical Review Letters | publisher=American Physical Society (APS) | volume=87 | issue=17 | date=3 October 2001 | issn=0031-9007 | doi=10.1103/physrevlett.87.176401 | article-number=176401| pmid=11690287 | bibcode=2001PhRvL..87q6401K }}</ref>
directly or by controlling their [[quantum dynamics]]. This research direction seems currently particularly lucrative due to the rapid progress of [[THz technology]] in producing high-quality, intense and/or single-cycle THz sources and lasers for spectroscopic purposes.

Stephan W. Koch's innovations have always caught broad interest within the research community; his papers have been cited more than 15000 times to date (2013).

==Awards==

Stephan W. Koch has received numerous awards for his achievements in the field of semiconductor optics. Most notably due to his work on the theoretical foundations of light–matter interaction in semiconductor materials, he received the [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz Prize|Leibniz Prize]] of the [[Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft]] in 1997 and the [[Max Planck Research Award]] of the [[Alexander von Humboldt Foundation]] and of the [[Max Planck Society]] in 1999.

==Books==

Stephan W. Koch has coauthored eight text books that have had a major effect on laying solid foundations to understand semiconductor optics and semiconductor [[quantum optics]]. His most recent work includes:

* {{cite book | last=Kira | first=Mackillo | title=Semiconductor quantum optics | publisher=Cambridge University Press | publication-place=Cambridge, UK New York | year=2012 | isbn=978-0-521-87509-7 | oclc=774110559}} [http://www.sqobook.org/ Website of this book (sqobook.org)]
* {{cite book | last=Haug | first=Hartmut | title=Quantum theory of the optical and electronic properties of semiconductors | publisher=World Scientific | publication-place=Singapore Hackensack, N.J | year=2009 | isbn=978-981-283-884-1 | oclc=297811039}}
* {{cite book | last=Meier | first=Torsten | title=Coherent semiconductor optics: from basic concepts to nanostructure applications | publisher=Springer | publication-place=Berlin New York | year=2007 | isbn=978-3-540-32555-0 | oclc=105375611}}
